cls: Prokinetic agent and antiemetic (dopamine D2 antagonist)
pharm: Central and peripheral dopamine D2 receptor antagonist; enhances upper GI motility and has antiemetic effect
quick: 10-15 mg PO up to 4 times daily, 30 min before meals and at bedtime; max 12 weeks
Take 30 minutes before meals (and at bedtime)
Use only if clearly needed; commonly used data do not show major risk
Excreted in milk; use with caution
Reduce dose in renal impairment (drug is renally cleared)
Use with caution; reduce dose in significant impairment
Extrapyramidal/tardive dyskinesia signs, mood, renal function, treatment duration
summary: Metoclopramide is a dopamine D2 antagonist with prokinetic and antiemetic properties. It is used short-term for symptomatic gastroesophageal reflux unresponsive to conventional therapy and for diabetic gastroparesis, as well as to prevent nausea and vomiting. It accelerates gastric emptying and increases lower esophageal sphincter tone. It carries a boxed warning for tardive dyskinesia, and treatment should generally not exceed 12 weeks.
indications: Short-term (4 to 12 weeks) therapy for adults with symptomatic, documented gastroesophageal reflux who fail to respond to conventional therapy
Relief of symptoms of acute and recurrent diabetic gastroparesis (diabetic gastric stasis)
Other formulations: prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting and chemotherapy-induced emesis, and to facilitate small-bowel intubation or radiologic examination

dosage.d: 10 to 15 mg up to 4 times daily, 30 minutes before each meal and at bedtime; intermittent symptoms may be treated with single doses up to 20 mg before the provoking situation
dosage.t: 30 minutes before meals; total therapy not to exceed 12 weeks
dosage.n: Elderly or more sensitive patients may need only 5 mg per dose

dosage.d: 10 mg 30 minutes before each meal and at bedtime for 2 to 8 weeks depending on response
dosage.n: Reinstitute if symptoms recur; do not exceed 12 weeks total

dosage.d: Reduce dose (approximately one-half) when creatinine clearance is below 40 mL/min

admin: Administer 30 minutes before meals and at bedtime for prokinetic effect
Limit total treatment duration to 12 weeks except in rare cases where benefit outweighs the risk of tardive dyskinesia
Reduce the dose in elderly patients and in renal impairment
Discontinue immediately if signs of tardive dyskinesia or extrapyramidal symptoms develop
For intravenous use, inject slowly over at least 1 to 2 minutes to avoid intense anxiety and restlessness
moa: Metoclopramide antagonizes dopamine D2 receptors. Peripherally it increases the response to acetylcholine in the upper gastrointestinal tract, enhancing gastric and small-bowel motility and raising lower esophageal sphincter tone, which accelerates gastric emptying and intestinal transit. Centrally, it blocks dopamine receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, producing an antiemetic effect. It does not stimulate gastric, biliary, or pancreatic secretions.

absolute: Situations where increased gastrointestinal motility is dangerous (GI hemorrhage, mechanical obstruction, or perforation)
Known hypersensitivity or intolerance to metoclopramide
Epilepsy or use with other drugs likely to cause extrapyramidal reactions (increased seizures/EPS)
monitor: Signs of tardive dyskinesia and extrapyramidal symptoms

preg: Available data have not established a drug-associated risk of major birth defects; metoclopramide is widely used in pregnancy for nausea and reflux. Use during pregnancy when clearly needed; neonatal exposure near delivery may rarely cause extrapyramidal or methemoglobinemia effects.
lact: Metoclopramide is excreted in human milk. Use with caution during breastfeeding, weighing the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need and any potential adverse effects on the infant.
renal: Metoclopramide is substantially eliminated by the kidney. Reduce the dose (approximately by half) in patients with creatinine clearance below 40 mL/min, and titrate cautiously, as accumulation increases the risk of extrapyramidal effects.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment, particularly with fluid retention or cirrhosis where metoclopramide may aggravate fluid overload; consider dose reduction.

major: Antipsychotics and other dopamine antagonists (additive extrapyramidal symptoms and neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk)
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (risk of hypertension from catecholamine release)
Drugs that prolong the QT interval (additive risk)
moderate: CNS depressants including alcohol, opioids, and sedatives (additive sedation)
Insulin (altered timing of food absorption may require insulin dose/timing adjustment)
minor: Drugs whose absorption depends on gastric transit (e.g., digoxin absorption decreased, cyclosporine absorption increased)
interactions.food: Take 30 minutes before meals for best prokinetic effect
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; it adds to sedation and CNS depression
interactions.diagnostics: May increase plasma aldosterone and prolactin; can transiently affect gastric emptying studies

serious: Acute dystonic reactions and extrapyramidal symptoms
rare: Fluid retention and heart failure exacerbation
emergency: Acute dystonia (involuntary muscle spasms of face, neck, tongue) - seek urgent care; treat with anticholinergic/diphenhydramine
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (high fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability) - stop drug and seek emergency care
Tardive dyskinesia (involuntary repetitive movements) - discontinue and seek evaluation

monitoring: Signs of tardive dyskinesia and other extrapyramidal symptoms at each visit
Total cumulative dose and duration of therapy (limit to 12 weeks)
Mood and emergence of depression or suicidal ideation
Blood pressure and, in neonates, signs of methemoglobinemia
counsel: Take 30 minutes before meals and at bedtime as directed; do not use longer than prescribed
Report any uncontrollable movements of the face, tongue, arms, or legs immediately
This medicine can cause drowsiness; avoid driving until you know how it affects you and avoid alcohol
Report new restlessness, depressed mood, or thoughts of self-harm
Tell your doctor about all medicines, including those for mental health and Parkinson disease
pk: Oral onset of GI effect in 30-60 minutes; intravenous 1-3 minutes
Peak plasma concentration about 1-2 hours after oral dosing
Approximately 5 to 6 hours (longer in renal impairment)
Prokinetic effect lasts about 1 to 2 hours per dose
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect oral solution from light
pearls: Boxed warning: can cause tardive dyskinesia, often irreversible; risk rises with duration and cumulative dose - avoid treatment beyond 12 weeks except in rare cases
Reduce the dose in the elderly and in renal impairment, where extrapyramidal risk is highest
Contraindicated in GI obstruction, perforation, hemorrhage, pheochromocytoma, and epilepsy
Acute dystonic reactions respond to anticholinergics or diphenhydramine
Avoid combining with antipsychotics and other dopamine antagonists
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember, before your next meal. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Symptoms of overdose include drowsiness, disorientation, and extrapyramidal reactions (dystonia, akathisia). Anticholinergic or antiparkinson drugs (e.g., diphenhydramine, benztropine) help control extrapyramidal symptoms; treatment is otherwise supportive, and methemoglobinemia is treated with methylene blue. Contact Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).
